title: The head start
caption:
Two loyalty cards. Same eight washes.
One of them got almost TWICE as many people to the finish.

The only difference? It came with two stamps already on it.

When the goal feels close, people run for it.
So never make anyone start at zero. Not in your onboarding, not in a long form, not in your loyalty program.

Where could you give the first step away?
Send this to whoever runs your site

title: The finish line
caption:
Card in hand. Last step.
And then shipping shows up out of nowhere.

Surprise costs are the number one reason people abandon a cart.
The fix is not a new feature. It's three small decisions...
Show the full price from the first screen.
Let guests buy with just an email.
Put the total on the button.

Nothing new to build. Just nothing left to surprise them.
Share this with someone who has a checkout

title: How we met
caption:
People ask how Two Otters started.

She was 15. He was 16.
She saw him standing outside the community centre and just started talking.

25 years and six projects together later...
she's still following him around. These days it's in Figma.

Otters hold hands so they don't drift apart.
Say hi, we'd love to know who's here

title: The first date
caption:
Imagine a first date who leans in for a kiss before you've even sat down.

Awkward, right?
That's most homepages. "Book a call" and "Buy now" before the visitor even knows what you do.

Trust takes time. But you can shorten it.
Open with their problem. Say what they get. Ask for the call once you've earned it.

Easy to say. Hard to do.
What's the first thing YOUR homepage asks for?

title: Four buttons, zero clicks
caption:
Book a call. Get the guide. Watch the video. Follow us.

Four buttons, all shouting at once.
So the eye doesn't know where to go, and it just leaves.

Ask what the page is really FOR.
That one thing gets the only filled button. The second choice gets an outline. Everything else becomes a text link, or goes.

One page. One job. One button that looks like it.
Send this to whoever built your landing page

title: Who's more likely to
caption:
Who's more likely to...

Remember every word from a meeting three years ago?
Want it perfect before anyone sees it?
Spend half of a one-hour meeting gossiping?

We pointed. We disagreed a little.

Now your turn.
Who would you point at on YOUR team?

title: Why no one clicked
caption:
"I don't need to tell my clients what to do. They already know me."

And then...
"Why did no one click on my link?"

People are not being difficult. They're busy.
If you want them to read, download or buy, say so. Clearly. Once.

That's not pushy. That's helpful.
Do you tell your audience what to do next?

title: One empty box
caption:
One optional box on a checkout form.
Twelve million dollars a year.

People didn't know what to type in it, so they guessed. The guess broke the payment.
The site deleted the box. The money came back.

Every field is one more question between your customer and paying you.
Go through your form and ask... do we really need this one?

Share this with whoever owns your forms

title: Why otters
caption:
Did you know otters hold hands while they sleep?
So the current doesn't pull them in different directions.

That's us.
Keren keeps the design from drifting away from the strategy.
Amir keeps the strategy from staying on paper.

And yes, we kept the bloopers.
Send this to the person who keeps you from drifting

title: Shh
caption:
That voice in your head that tells you that you can't.
The one that keeps you in bed a little longer and makes excuses for you.

Shh.

Save this for the next morning it gets loud

title: A tenth of a second
source_name: Reel E - A tenth of a second.mp4
caption:
How fast does your site need to be?
Faster than you think.

When mobile sites loaded a tenth of a second faster, shoppers bought 8% more.
That's about one blink.

And it's rarely technical magic. It's huge images, and apps and pop-ups nobody remembers adding.
Shrink. Remove. Then test on a phone, not on the office wifi.

Send this to whoever looks after your site

title: What clients say vs what we hear
caption:
What clients say. And what we hear.

"I want a clean, beautiful site."
We hear... nobody stopped to decide what the main message is.

"I want a site that blows people away."
We hear... they want to be remembered. Which is not the same as animation everywhere.

"I want to set a new standard for my industry."
That one is our favourite. Because that takes strategy AND design.

Which one have you said?

title: Five signs your site needs a refresh
caption:
Five signs your website needs a refresh...

It was built more than a year ago.
Your offer has changed.
It doesn't reflect what you actually do.
The traffic isn't coming.
The design feels old.

One of them is enough.
How many did you count?

title: Ten seconds
caption:
You get about ten seconds.
And in those ten seconds your visitor is asking one thing...
Is this for me?

"Welcome to our website" doesn't answer it.
Neither does "Solutions for tomorrow".

Your headline should say what you do, who it's for, and why you.
Show it to a stranger for five seconds. If they can't tell you what you sell, rewrite it.

Share this with someone who's about to launch

title: The project we'd do differently
caption:
There's a project we'd run completely differently today.

Every draft got approved. No questions, no notes.
It felt great. It should have been a red flag.

Because when it reached development, the changes arrived all at once.

Not everyone knows how to give feedback. So now it's built into our process...
a guided conversation where we go through the work together, before the revision round.

That's why we work in a spiral.
Save this for your next project

title: Charge by value
caption:
Still charging by the hour?

Three questions that might change that...
What shortcut am I offering my clients?
How do I contribute to their success?
How can I present what I do better?

An hour is the same for everyone. Your value isn't.
Save this for your next proposal

title: The option nobody wants
caption:
Want more people to pick your best package?
Add one that nobody wants.

Three subscriptions. One of them made no sense, and nobody chose it.
But next to it, the best package looked like a steal, and 84% took it.

A price on its own means nothing.
People need something to compare it to.

Send this to whoever writes your pricing page

title: Meet the otters
caption:
Tired of suppliers who hand you something generic?

Meet Amir. He scans any site, platform or app in seconds and tells you what to change so it feels intuitive.
Meet Keren. Strategy that hears what you DIDN'T say.

We tried to introduce each other properly.
It went about as well as you'd expect.

Say hi in the comments

title: How to get noticed
caption:
There's someone in your niche you'd love to get in front of.

Here's the short guide...
Introduce yourself, but mostly tell them what you love about THEIR work.
Offer something they need, or a connection worth having.
Show them what they gain by picking you.
And make it easy. Don't send them searching. Send the link.

Who would you write to first?

title: Five reviews
caption:
Not five hundred reviews.
Five.

A product with five reviews is 270% more likely to sell than a product with none.
People don't need to be convinced. They need to see they're not the first.

So ask your happy customers today.
And put the reviews right next to the button, where people decide.

Share this with someone who's hiding their reviews on a separate page

title: What we won't do
caption:
A few things we won't do.

Send you a 20-page questionnaire, then ask the same questions again on the call.
Move forward without asking what's really bothering you.
Hand you something generic that ignores your business goals.
Treat your project like one more tick on a production line.
Keep a good idea to ourselves.

That's the list.
What would you add to it?

title: Brand voice
caption:
Some brands feel like a person.
They have a character. A way of doing things.

That's brand voice.
Voice is WHAT you keep saying to your audience. Tone is HOW you say it.

And it doesn't matter how big you are.
A small brand with a clear voice is easier to remember than a big one without it.

If your brand were a person, how would it talk?

title: The first hour
caption:
Someone just filled in your contact form.
How long until you call them back?

Reply within the first hour and you're nearly seven times more likely to get a real conversation.
Wait a day and it's like they never asked.

Set an instant reply. Put a real time on it.
Then keep the promise.

Send this to whoever answers your leads

title: Same question, same second
caption:
Same question. Same second.

What keeps clients coming back?
How much should you give a client?
What's the best way to start a project?
When do we show the client?

Turns out we agree on everything that matters.
Almost.

Try it with your business partner and tell us how it went

title: No struggle, no story
caption:
What if Simba had been born and crowned king on the same day?

Nobody would have watched.

Same goes for your brand.
No struggle, no development, no reason to follow.

So ask yourself...
What is it in your brand's journey that makes it worth your audience's time?

That's the part people remember.
Tell us yours in the comments

title: Everything asks for attention
caption:
Every banner, every badge, every little line of text is asking your customer for attention.
And attention runs out fast.

So ask one question about every element on the page...
Does this help someone decide?
If not, move it or lose it.

Less on the screen means more of it gets SEEN.
Share this with someone whose homepage is shouting

title: Where every project starts
caption:
Every project starts in the same place.

Not with a logo. Not with a colour.
With strategy.

Also, this took us a few takes.
Send this to someone who starts with the logo

title: The bridge
caption:
Let's learn from great brands.
Today... the bridge.

Show the problem.
Show the reality people want.
Then place your product as the way across.

A classic toothpaste ad did it with one question from a teacher to her class. A month apart, the answer changed.

Problem on one side. Desired reality on the other. You are the bridge.
What's on each side of yours?

title: The finish line you can see
caption:
Why does a coffee card make you buy more coffee?

The closer people get to the free one, the faster they come back.
The finish line pulls them in.

Your site can do the same.
A progress bar on a long form. Or simply "two more steps and you're done".

When people can see the end, they get there.
Send this to whoever owns your sign-up flow

title: The brothers
caption:
Let's learn from great brands.

A younger brother who just wants his big brother to notice him.
A whole ad of suspense. And then the big brother shows up.

Yes, there's a bottle in the scene.
But what you remember is the family.

That's storytelling that carries your values instead of listing them.
Which value would your brand's story be about?

title: "Are you sure?"
caption:
"Are you sure?"
Sure about WHAT, exactly?

That pop-up shows up right before something big happens, and tells your customer almost nothing.

Say what's about to happen. Say whose it is. Say if it can't be undone.

Nobody deletes the wrong thing.
And nobody calls support to fix it.

Share this with whoever writes your pop-ups

title: Everyone's an athlete
caption:
Let's learn from great brands.

This one sees every person as a potential athlete.
Not only the champions. The guy who runs and just doesn't give up. The woman who runs while the neighbours stare.

World-class athletes next to everyday people.
That's a story we can ALL find ourselves in.

Who is the hero in your brand's story?

title: Yes or no
caption:
Yes. No.
Two little words that cause a lot of mistakes.

When a button just says "Yes", people have to go back and read the question.
Most of them don't. They just click.

So write the action on the button.
"Delete order". "Keep my order".

When the button says what it does, nobody clicks by accident.
Send this to your product person

title: Hand them the mic
caption:
Let's learn from great brands.

A hygiene brand that could have talked about products.
Instead, it let real women tell their own stories. Unpolished. Unapologetic.

The brand didn't take the stage. It handed over the mic.
That's what makes it memorable, relatable and worth following.

Where could your brand step back and let your audience speak?

title: "Success!"
caption:
"Success!"
Great. But what actually happened?

Say it plainly. "Your address was updated."
And put an Undo right next to it.

That little Undo tells people they can't break anything.
People who feel safe try things. And people who feel safe are the ones who buy.

Share this with whoever writes your messages

title: Nine pairs
caption:
Keren here.

When I lived in the States I fell in love with a shoe brand.
Comfortable, colourful, vegan options. An easy choice.

But what made me buy them again and again?
For every pair I bought, a child in need got a pair too.
Nine pairs. Nine children.

I wasn't buying shoes. I was buying how it made me feel about myself.
What does buying from YOU say about your customer?

title: Let the picture sell
caption:
Online, nobody can touch your product.
So the picture has to do all the work.

And on most product cards, it gets squeezed. Badges, prices, buttons and long names all fighting for the same space.

Give the image most of the card.
Big. Clean. Room to breathe.

When the product looks better, people stop comparing you on price.
Send this to someone with an online store

title: Storytelling vs business storytelling
caption:
Storytelling took over marketing.
But what's the difference between storytelling and BUSINESS storytelling?

Thank you for asking.

Storytelling is building the right flow to land a message.
Business storytelling is how your brand story shows up everywhere. Your values, your messages and your visuals, working as one voice.

One is a skill. The other is a system.
Save this for the next time someone says "we need a story"

title: Three prices
caption:
Three prices on one little card.
Together they don't say quality. They say clearance sale.

Show ONE price.
Keep the name to one line.
Let the details wait on the product page.

A calm card looks like a better product.
And a better product doesn't need to shout about discounts.

Share this with someone who loves a sale badge

title: Strategy is not a calendar
caption:
"Strategy" has become a filler word.

A content calendar is not a content strategy.
The calendar is planning. It comes AFTER.

Strategy answers the harder questions first...
Who are you talking to?
What's the goal?
How will you get there, why are you doing it, and when should you see results?

And yes, a brand can have more than one.
Mind-blowing, we know

title: The tiny button
caption:
Your customer taps the product photo.
Nothing happens.

Because the only thing that works is a tiny button in the corner.
That's a lost sale, one tap at a time.

Make the whole card clickable. The image, the name, the price.
Wherever the finger lands, it should go to the product.

Send this to whoever built your store

title: The site with no story
source_name: Remake 16 - The site with no story.mp4
caption:
A big brand. A big website.
And no story.

Just one patch on top of another. No clear voice. Generic.

A clear message matters. But what makes it count is how the visitor FEELS, and whether your solution becomes the one for their pain.

For that you need a journey.
The main message, the hidden ones, the flow, the UX and the visuals. Together.

Does your site tell a story, or list things?

title: A thumb is not a mouse
caption:
Your site was designed on a big screen, with a mouse.
Your customers are using a thumb.

And a thumb is not a mouse.
Tiny buttons get missed. The wrong thing gets tapped. People give up.

Give everything tappable a generous area, even when the icon itself is small.

Easy to hit saves your customer the frustration, and saves you the customer.
Share this with your designer

title: The Israeli kitchen
caption:
Awkward question.
What makes Israeli cuisine so good?

It's the mix. Many cultures on one plate.

Marketing works the same way.
It's never "I just need to know this one thing".
It's content, branding, sales, design, UX and client psychology, meeting in one place.

Only the mix comes out amazing.
That's why we put strategy and design at the same table

title: Grey on white
caption:
Light grey text on a white background.
So elegant on the designer's screen.

Then your customer opens it on a phone, outside, at noon.
And it's gone.

Keep body text at a readable size and make the contrast strong.
If people have to squint, they scroll right past.

Readable is always more elegant than invisible.
Send this to someone who loves light grey

title: Saying no
caption:
Keren here.

I once said no to a $13,000 project.
An interesting brief. A full brand and story to build.

But the further I got, the clearer it became that the work went against what I believe in.
And once I saw that, saying no was easy.

I would have said yes if money mattered more to me than compassion.
Luckily, it didn't.

What would you say no to?

title: Red and green
caption:
One in twelve men can't easily tell red from green.

So when your form only turns a field red, a lot of people simply don't see it.
They press submit again. And again. And then they leave.

Always pair the colour with a sign.
An icon, and a short line that says exactly what's missing.

Then everyone knows what to fix, and the form gets sent.
Share this with whoever owns your forms
